name: Blue Lagoon
label: Blue Lagoon
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/69991144: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Blue Lagoon' (158 m across).
notes: Iceland's famous milky-blue geothermal spa set in a black lava field.

text.description: The Blue Lagoon is a geothermal spa set in a black lava field on the Reykjanes Peninsula, in front of Mount Þorbjörn. It is man-made. The water is a by-product of the nearby Svartsengi geothermal power station, and its milky blue colour comes from the silica in it. The soft white silica mud on the bottom adds to the pale look. That colour against dark volcanic rock is what makes it so easy to photograph, even on a phone. Steam drifting over the surface adds mood and depth to a shot. Bathing facilities opened in 1987, and the lagoon is now one of the most visited attractions in Iceland. It is about 20 km from Keflavík International Airport. The area has also seen volcanic activity since late 2023. Lava reached the site in November 2024 and destroyed the car park, but protective barriers kept the lagoon itself intact, and the site has closed and reopened several times since. For photos, keep the dark lava, the blue water and the sky in the frame together, and use the steam as a soft foreground. Keep your phone dry and wipe the lens often, because steam and splashes leave marks. Check the official site for current opening and access before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Blue Lagoon sits in a lava field on the Reykjanes Peninsula, about 5 km from Grindavík, in front of Mount Þorbjörn and beside the Svartsengi geothermal power station.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot. The lagoon is about 5 km from Grindavík and about 20 km from Keflavík International Airport. Lava destroyed the car park in November 2024 and a new car park was being built, so check the official site for how to get there before you travel. The phone icon on the map is about 10 m south of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole lagoon, the lava and the mountain. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, more natural look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out people in the water, steam patterns or the edge of the lava.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 10 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Stay on the paths and in the areas open to visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the upper third line so the milky water fills most of the frame. Include a strip of dark lava in the foreground for contrast. Wait for gaps in the steam so the colour shows through.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the water to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pale blue keeps its colour and the white steam does not wash out. Wipe the lens with a dry cloth before each shot, as steam leaves a haze on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light on an overcast day suits the milky blue. Low sun early or late in the day adds warmth and shadows on the lava. In the dark months, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a rail or wall.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed spa and its opening has been affected by volcanic activity, so check the official site before you go.

name: Grindavík
label: Grindavík town
notes: Fishing town on the Reykjanes peninsula, affected by the recent volcanic activity.

text.description: Grindavík is a working fishing town on the far south-western tip of the Reykjanes Peninsula, and it is one of the few places on this coast with a proper harbour. That is the main reason to photograph it. You get low buildings, boats and working quays set against an old lava field and open sky, so the picture says something about life here. The town stands on an old lava field, and the harbour, called Hópið, only became the town's fishing base in 1939, when locals dug a channel through a reef to link it to the sea. A lighthouse built in 1928 stands on the southern tip of the nearby peninsula, and it makes a good small detail if you can see it. The Blue Lagoon is about 5 kilometres away. Volcanic activity since late 2023 has affected the town, and parts of it have been evacuated at different times, so the situation on the ground may differ from older photos. Keep to any signs and closures, and do not cross barriers for a better angle. Frame the roofs and harbour with the wide sky around them, and include the lava ground if it is visible. Keep any people or private property incidental rather than the main subject.
text.geographic_location: Grindavík is a fishing town on the far south-western Reykjanes Peninsula in Iceland's Southern Peninsula district, near the hill Þorbjörn.
text.directions_text: No railway or tram stops are listed for this spot, so check current local travel options and the access status before you set out. From there, the town is about 7 minutes on foot (580 m) to the north-west. Check the latest local advice first, as access has changed during recent volcanic activity. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the town as you see it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the sky and the surrounding landscape in the frame, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the harbour, boats or lighthouse from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Grindavíkurhöfn (harbour waterfront). The working harbour waterfront of the fishing town, with the boats and harbour buildings in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. If the lava ground is visible, keep a strip of it in the foreground to give a sense of place, and let the rooftops and any boats sit in the middle band. If you can see the lighthouse, include it as a small detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and any lava ground does not turn muddy. Try a panorama if you want the full sweep of the town, and hold the phone steady and level as you turn.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, lower light on the buildings and the landscape. On bright days around midday the sky can look washed out.

text.access_note: The town has been affected by volcanic activity and evacuations since late 2023, so check the official site before you go to find out which areas are open.

name: Þorbjörn
label: Þorbjörn mountain
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Grindavíkurvegur' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Grindavíkurvegur nearest the subject (our map tiles).
notes: Hill above the Blue Lagoon with hiking trails and views over the lava fields.

text.description: Þorbjörn is a 243 m volcanic mountain right beside Grindavík, on the Reykjanes peninsula. It is not tall, but it stands alone beside the town and the Svartsengi area, so it fills a phone frame easily and reads clearly against the sky. It grew from eruptions under a glacier during a cold spell in the Pleistocene, and a long split runs across the top, forming a small canyon up to 80 m deep. The small canyon in the mountain is called Þjófagjá, or Thieves' Canyon, after an old story of bandits caught by a farmer's son. There is also a jeep track up the slope, built by the U.S. Army during World War II, and radio and television masts now stand on the summit. From the top you can see the Blue Lagoon. The easiest picture for most visitors is the approach view from Grindavíkurvegur, on the stretch heading into town from the Blue Lagoon side, where the mountain rises beside the road. Take it as a wide, simple frame: road in the foreground, mountain as the main shape, sky above. If you are fit and the path is open, the summit gives a second kind of photo looking down over the town, the Atlantic and the Blue Lagoon, with the radio buildings in the foreground. The mountain has seen ground movement and earthquakes since 2020, so check current access and closure notices before heading up.
text.geographic_location: Þorbjörn sits just outside Grindavík on the Reykjanes peninsula, between the town and the Svartsengi power station and Blue Lagoon area. Road 43 runs on its eastern side, and route 426 curves round its western side.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot, and no public transport is listed, so it is easiest reached by road. Check the road on a map before stopping, and use a safe pull-in rather than the carriageway. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the road, the mountain and the sky together. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, as it makes the mountain look smaller. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out the summit buildings and the ridge line.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Grindavíkurvegur (stretch heading into Grindavík from the Blue Lagoon side, mountain on the left). Þorbjörn rising beside the road with the approach to Grindavík in view. Face north-west toward the mountain, and the photo shows Þorbjörn rising beside the road. Do not stand in the road: use a safe verge or pull-in, and keep away from moving traffic.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the mountain on one third of the frame, with the road leading the eye into the picture. Keep the horizon level, as the mountain's slopes look best with a straight skyline. If you go up the mountain instead, shoot back over Grindavík and the Atlantic with the summit's radio buildings in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the mountain's slope to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the slope keeps its colour and detail. Take a few shots, as passing cars can ruin a frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the sun is low and the mountain's slopes show relief; the early morning or the hours before sunset are usually kinder than flat midday light.

text.access_note: The view from the road is from a public road, but check current access and closure notices before walking up the mountain.

name: Svartsengi Power Station
label: Svartsengi Power Stn
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9091413: large area 'Svartsengi Power Station' (612 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Steaming geothermal plant beside the Blue Lagoon that feeds the lagoon's water.

text.description:
Svartsengi is a working geothermal power station set in a bare, dark lava landscape, and that contrast is what makes it photograph well. Pipes, buildings and drifting steam sit against black rock and a wide Icelandic sky. The name means 'black meadow', which suits the setting.

The plant was built in 1976 and was the world's first to combine electricity generation with hot water for district heating. It grew in six phases, finished in 2008, and now covers about 150 hectares. It can produce 75 MW of electricity. Its hot water heats more than 21,000 households across the Reykjanes Peninsula, so the plant matters to everyday life here. The Blue Lagoon is a spin-off of the same geothermal field.

During the recent eruptions near Grindavík, earth barriers were built around the plant to protect it from lava. That adds a little human-scale drama to the story you are photographing.

For your phone, the plant looks best as a layered scene. Put dark ground in the foreground, the buildings and pipework in the middle, and steam and sky behind. Keep the horizon level with the gridlines on. Because the plant is a few hundred metres away, a zoomed shot will pick out detail better than a wide one. A wider shot helps if you want to show the whole sweep of the site against the lava.

The area has been affected by volcanic activity, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Svartsengi lies in the Svartsengi geothermal field, about 4 km north of Grindavík on the Reykjanes Peninsula. The Blue Lagoon is a spin-off of the same geothermal field.
text.directions_text: Start from Grindavík and head about 4 km north towards the Svartsengi geothermal field. Roads here have been affected by recent eruptions, so check the official site before you go. The phone icon on the map is about 350 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole scene. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for pipes, chimneys and steam. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you can place dark rock or a path in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 350 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Use the dark ground as a foreground band and let the buildings and steam sit above it. At 2x or 3x the plant looks more compact and the layers stack neatly. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky and steam keep their detail and the dark lava does not wash out. Hold the phone steady with both hands when zoomed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the sun is low, gives the best modelling on the buildings and steam. Cold, still, clear days usually make the steam easier to see.

text.access_note: The plant is an operating industrial site, so view it from a public place and check the official site before you go, as access around Grindavík may be restricted because of volcanic activity.
